questions.q: In the pipeline this lesson walks through, what is the very first step after a developer makes a change?
options: Committing the change to one object's script and opening a pull request
Deploying directly to production without review
Running smoke tests against production data
Building a DACPAC and deploying it immediately, with no code review
questions.explain: The sequence begins with a commit and a pull request, before any automated validation or deployment happens.

questions.q: What stops the pipeline immediately if the schema doesn't build cleanly?
options: The CI build stage — everything downstream depends on it succeeding first
Nothing; a failed build is ignored and deployment continues
Only a human manually watching the pipeline can stop it
The rollback stage, which runs before the build stage
questions.explain: Each stage in the pipeline depends on the previous one succeeding, so a failed CI build halts everything before deployment.

questions.q: At what stage does the pipeline apply migrations to a genuinely disposable test database and run smoke tests?
options: After the change deploys to a test environment, before it ever reaches production
After the change has already been deployed to production
Before the pull request is even opened
This lesson's pipeline has no testing stage at all
questions.explain: Testing happens against a throwaway test database after deployment to test, and before production deployment.

questions.q: In the conceptual YAML pipeline shown in this lesson, what does the `needs:` field enforce?
options: That a stage only runs if the stage(s) it depends on succeeded first
The exact runtime, in seconds, a stage is allowed to take
Which developer is allowed to approve a given stage
The programming language used to write the migration scripts
questions.explain: The needs: dependency declaration is what enforces stage ordering and gates later stages on earlier success.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about the realism of the pipeline it describes?
options: It requires nothing beyond infrastructure the chapter already covered — database projects, Git, build/deploy mechanics, test databases, and a rollback plan
It's a simplified fantasy that wouldn't work in a real environment
It requires a specialized, unnamed proprietary product not otherwise covered in the course
It only applies to NoSQL databases, not SQL Server
questions.explain: The walkthrough deliberately uses only tools and concepts already taught earlier in the chapter, making it an honest, realistic description.
